set.signal: Q3 FY2026 revenue $650M, +8% YoY, but ~$90M BELOW the expectations given on the Q2 call — CFO Ahmed Pasha: the shortfall was primarily production delays at two new contract-manufacturing facilities that are ramping. Adjusted gross profit also carried ~$15M of costs for new-product rollout and the production delays, plus a $15M loss recorded on a planned long-term battery supply agreement (mostly one project). CEO Julian Nebreda: excluding some of the one-time costs of the year, margin 'will have been around the 12% that we guided', Fluence is 'still very comfortably within the 10%-15% range', and backlog and new orders are in line with 10%-15%; on the margin pressure a larger storage supplier announced, the CEO said 'We do not understand the pressure that the other big supplier announced' ('It might be something in their cost structure that is different'). CFO: implied Q4 gross margin roughly 11%.

items.reason: '(Apr-Jun)' is not stated; the CEO said he does not understand the peer's margin pressure (not that Fluence does not see it); the 11% Q4 margin is the CFO's figure (the analyst had suggested ~12%).
items.evidence: We do not understand the pressure that the other big supplier announced that they were coming out with this.

CFO: the $60M EBITDA reduction is largely ~$44M of lost margin on the ~$400M of revenue shifted into 2027 plus $15M related to the proposed long-term battery supply agreement; Fluence expects to realize the revenues of the delayed Q3 projects. ARR of ~$180M by FY2026-end MAINTAINED. CFO: implied Q4 gross margin roughly 11%; CEO: roughly half of what Fluence needs to do for Q4 was already produced and fully integrated at the time of the call. Fiscal-YTD orders $2.7B, 80% higher than last year, with utilities and IPPs ~90% of the total. Pipeline exited the quarter at $33.1B (+$1.6B QoQ, which CEO Julian Nebreda said indicates $3B of new opportunities after conversions), with a growing U.S. share mostly attributed to data centers. Backlog coverage for FY2027 is ~$2.2B as of June 30 vs the $1.5B of FY2026 coverage as of June 30, 2025; CEO on 2027 coverage: 'I still believe that 80%-90% is the right one, the 85%'. CEO: the ~$1.1B of non-data-center orders split around 60% U.S. / 40% international, which 'doesn't mean that that's what this is going to be'.

items.reason: '~$2.8B for the year after' is the analyst's (Vikram Bagri) number, not management's; hedge on the 60/40 split restored.
items.evidence: backlog converting $2.2 billion next year, $2.8 billion after that. Pretty long-dated backlog at this point.

set.signal: FIRST data-center orders and awards, totaling $850M (CEO Julian Nebreda). (1) A $300M order for a BEHIND-THE-METER project — Fluence's first deal with a data-center developer — referred by one of the two hyperscalers Fluence holds MSAs with; the developer is building a data center for one of the hyperscalers. Lead-to-order took three months ('less than three months'), which the CEO called much faster than Fluence's traditional market segment; the CEO expects data-center work to have a much faster conversion cycle, while the other ~90% of the business keeps its conversion cycle of roughly a year to 18 months. (2) ~$550M of awards in July across MULTIPLE data-center sites under one of the two hyperscaler MSAs (a tender) — 'These are not yet purchase orders'; Fluence is finalizing the final technical points and expects conversion into backlog in the coming months. Data-center pipeline grew to 16 GWh, a more than 35% increase vs Q2, a mix of hyperscalers (the majority) and developers (the growing segment). CEO: hyperscalers focus on QUALITY of power (load smoothing, low-voltage ride-through via Fluence's operating system); developers on SPEED-TO-POWER. Data-center projects have a duration of two hours, and between developer and hyperscaler deals there is no real difference in technical requirements and 'the margins of them generally very much align'. Manufacturing delays do NOT affect the MSAs — they concern contracts signed 'a year, a year and a half ago'.
set.figure: $850M data-center total = $300M BTM developer order + ~$550M July hyperscaler awards; DC pipeline 16 GWh (>35% QoQ); 2 MSAs with 2 hyperscalers; 2-hour duration

items.reason: These are orders / awards, not revenue; the 12-18 month figure is the revenue conversion cycle of the rest of the book, not a lead-to-order time; 'same hyperscaler' is not stated; margins align between developer and hyperscaler deals, not 'with the rest of the book'; pipeline growth was 'more than 35%'.
items.evidence: Our normal, the other 90% today or our other segments are working on the same conversion cycle of roughly a year to 18 months that we had.

items.label: Fluence Energy Q3 FY2026 (08-06-2026)
items.signal_prefix: SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. Two new contract-manu

set.signal: SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. Two new contract-manufacturing sites missed: (1) Houston, USA — a new, fully automated enclosure facility with expected capacity of 15 GWh per year that Fluence off-takes, run by the SAME contract manufacturer that has been its main enclosure supplier from Vietnam. Delayed a few months by construction, automation-equipment issues and a delay in the utility connection (the plant has been running on generators, so not all work could run in parallel); limited production started in Q3, grid connection expected 'in the next couple of weeks', FULL production expected in fiscal Q1 2027. (2) One of two new facilities in China — initial production of Smartstack components (CEO: the pods 'that go on top of the skids') did not meet Fluence's standards and required rework; corrections are implemented, shipping has resumed and CFO Ahmed Pasha said the facility has achieved full production in the fourth quarter. CEO: the plan carried a hedge and a contingency and the delays went over both. Organizational response: new leadership of supply chain and manufacturing reporting directly to the CEO, framed as an execution issue ('It's not a strategic change, it's an execution issue'), not a change of suppliers. CEO: once Houston is fully running, 'we expect to have capacity to meet our current backlog of projects and confidence to meet the growth of the U.S. market'.

items.reason: Personnel names / bios dropped (personnel changes are not captured); the CEO said capacity to meet the current backlog, not 'domestic-content capacity sufficient for its entire current backlog'.
items.evidence: Once it is fully run and added to our current supply chain, we expect to have capacity to meet our current backlog of projects and confidence to meet the growth of the U.S. market.
